chunks: "At minimum you need five things. First, power: a positive supply pin and a negative supply pin, which can be a negative rail or just ground in a single-supply design.
Second, the two inputs, which both need a defined DC voltage, so neither is left floating, because the inputs draw a tiny bias current and a floating pin will drift to a rail.
For a linear amplifier I also need the fourth thing, a feedback path from the output back to the inverting input, usually a resistor, because without it the op-amp is a comparator.
The fifth thing is the one people forget: a decoupling capacitor, typically 100 nanofarads ceramic, right next to the supply pins, plus a bigger bulk cap nearby.
It provides the fast current the output stage needs and keeps supply noise out of the signal.

Then I'd check the limits: the inputs have to stay inside the common-mode range, the output can't go outside the rails, and in a single-supply circuit I bias the signal to mid-supply so it can swing both ways.
In a dual or quad package I'd also tie off any unused channels instead of leaving them floating."
